place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the long dormitory bed

setup.zh: 腊月初八的夜。周衡结了「另议」那一笔；钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，你去赎那张弓。夜里，孙二狗摸到你铺前。
setup.en: The night of the eighth of the twelfth month. Zhou Heng settles the 'to be settled'; Money-Keeper Qian is packing up under the pagoda tree, and you go to redeem the bow. In the night, Sun Ergou creeps to your bunk.

recap.zh: 大比那夜，周衡结了巡夜那一笔，十块灵石；你赎回了爷爷的弓，利钱三十文是阿禾掏的。孙二狗说：「是你拉的。」你给家里写了第一封信：「娘，漏勺也能打水。」夜里银月说，镜子裂的那一下，那头有人：「叫徐州那个，十月去邺城等着。」
recap.en: The night of the contest, Zhou Heng settled the night-watch account — ten stones; you redeemed your grandfather's bow, and A He paid the thirty cash interest. Sun Ergou said: "You pulled me up." You wrote your first letter home: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too." In the night Yinyue said someone was at the other end of the mirror when it cracked: "Send the one from Xu. Tenth month, to Ye, to wait."

zh: 「叫徐州那个，十月去邺城等着。」
en: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too."
"Send the one from Xu. Tenth month, to Ye, to wait."

story.zh:
天黑下来的时候，周衡在执事房里点上了那半根蜡烛。小满进去的时候，他已经翻开了巡夜簿，拿指头点着一行一行往下念：「十月初一至初九，药园丢灵草十株。初八起，沈小满巡夜；初十以后，一株没丢，外加灵兽一只，狰，入册。另议的那一笔，今天议——」他从抽屉里一块一块地往外数，数一块，拿笔在账上划一道，「——一、二、三……十块。」数完了，又道：「记账。」

小满看着那十块灵石：「周师兄，晌午……」周衡道：「晌午你是来借。外门的账，不借。腊八结账，结在晚上，晌午说过了。」他把账簿合上，难得多说了一句：「《礼记》上说，古时候天子年底祭『蜡』，连吃田鼠的猫都请来谢。用过人家的，一定要还。连猫的账，都结。」小满把灵石揣进怀里，走到门口，回过头来叫了一声：「……周师兄。」周衡道：「嗯。」小满说：「有前途。」周衡咳嗽一声，挥挥手，叫他滚了。

钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，算盘还没收进袖子，看见阿禾过来，从怀里摸出一个小纸包，放在秤盘上称了一称，递给她：「阿禾姑娘。一文，一赔一百——你押的时候，板上写的是一赔一百。后来我要往上改，没改成，那是后来的事，跟你不相干。一百文，你数一数。」阿禾打开纸包，一文一文地数，数到一百，一文不多，一文不少。

小满跟着到了，把十块灵石放在秤盘上，又把当票放上去。钱掌柜一块一块地数了，把当票撕了，从木板背面摘下那张弓：「十块。利钱，三十文。」小满站在那里，没有动。他身上一文钱也没有。

阿禾没说话，从刚数完的那一百文里，又一文一文地数出三十文来，放在秤盘上。钱掌柜看了她一眼，收了，把弓递给小满。收摊的一个老弟子咂了咂嘴：「钱半文，钱半文。多一文不要，差半文不卖——这名号，倒不是白叫的。」钱掌柜把秤杆往肩上一扛，走了几步，回过头来冲小满道：「沈小满。明年还押你。」他又看了一眼那张弓，「那木头，你要是哪天打听出名字来，告诉我一声。不收钱。」

小满背上弓，道：「……他不是从来不认账的么？」阿禾道：「人人都这么说，可人人都没押中过。没押中过的人说他不认账，这话能信么？押中的人才知道。押中的人，又都不说。」那一文钱，是她娘缝在她衣角里的，初七那天她拿剪子挑开了线。她把剩下的七十文包好，塞进袖子里：「七十文，寄家，给弟弟。」顿了一顿，又道，「你今天没藏。」小满没说话，右手攥着，没有张开。她翻开小本子记了一行，**三十文。利息：不收**，合上本子，只说了两个字：「藏好。」

那天夜里，人都睡下了以后，孙二狗摸到了小满的铺位跟前，蹲了好一会儿，才小声道：「沈师兄。第一轮……你是故意输给我的吧？」小满道：「不是。我脚滑。」孙二狗道：「五行台上的石头，是干的。」小满道：「我脚汗多。」孙二狗便不说话了。他从腰里解下那个蓝布包，断了的那根绳子，他已经拿线接上了，接得歪歪扭扭。他道：「沈师兄，我今天……倒了七回。我娘说，人倒了不丢人，倒了不起来才丢人。」他咧嘴笑了一下，扯着下巴上的伤，嘶了一口气，「台上倒了七回，起来了七回。下了台，在石阶上坐下去那一回……我是真起不来了。是你拉的。」小满没有说话。黑暗里，他听见孙二狗摸回了自己的铺位，躺下去的时候，还小声地念叨了一句：「……记着了。」隔了一会儿，黑地里又传来他的声音：「沈师兄，你会写字吧？」小满道：「会几个。」孙二狗道：「明天……你替我写一封信。我娘不识字，村里有个先生会念。你就写：娘，我赢了一场。」他顿了一顿，「别写是怎么赢的。」
story.en:
At nightfall Zhou Heng lit the half candle in the stewards' office. When Xiaoman came in he already had the night-watch book open and was reading down it line by line with a finger: "First to ninth of the tenth month, ten herbs lost from the garden. From the eighth, Shen Xiaoman on night watch; after the tenth, not one lost, plus one spirit beast, a zheng, entered in the register. The 'to be settled' — settled today." He counted stones out of the drawer one by one, striking a line in the book for each: "— one, two, three… ten." Done, he said: "Entered."

Xiaoman looked at the ten stones. "Brother Zhou, at noon…" "At noon you came to borrow," said Zhou Heng. "The outer court doesn't lend. Laba accounts close in the evening — I said so at noon." He shut the ledger and, for once, said one thing more: "The Book of Rites says that at year's end the Son of Heaven held the Zha rite and thanked even the cats that ate the field mice. What you've used of someone else's, you must pay back. Even the cats' accounts are settled." Xiaoman tucked the stones into his coat, went to the door, and turned back. "…Brother Zhou." "Mm." "You've got a future." Zhou Heng coughed and waved him out.

Money-Keeper Qian was packing up under the pagoda tree, his abacus not yet in his sleeve. Seeing A He come, he took a small paper packet from his coat, weighed it on the scale and handed it to her: "Miss A He. One cash, one to a hundred — when you bet, the board said one to a hundred. Later I meant to raise it and didn't; that's later, nothing to do with you. A hundred cash — count it." She opened it and counted coin by coin to a hundred, not one more, not one less.

Xiaoman came up behind her and put the ten stones on the scale pan, and the pawn ticket on top. Qian counted the stones one by one, tore up the ticket, and took the bow down from the back of the board: "Ten. Interest, thirty cash." Xiaoman stood there and didn't move. He hadn't a single cash on him.

A He said nothing. From the hundred cash she had just counted she counted out thirty more, one by one, and laid them on the scale pan. Qian looked at her, took them, and handed the bow to Xiaoman. A senior packing up nearby smacked his lips: "Qian Half-Cash, Qian Half-Cash. Won't take a cash over, won't sell a half-cash under — he's earned the name." Qian shouldered his steelyard, walked a few steps, and looked back at Xiaoman: "Shen Xiaoman. I'll bet on you next year." He glanced at the bow once more. "That wood — if you ever find out its name, tell me. No charge."

Xiaoman slung the bow on. "…Didn't they say he never pays?" "Everyone says so, and nobody's ever won. People who never won say he doesn't pay — can you believe that? Only the winners know. And the winners don't talk." That one cash her mother had sewn into her hem; on the seventh she'd snipped the thread. She wrapped up the seventy cash left and tucked them into her sleeve: "Seventy cash, sent home, for my brother." A pause. "You didn't hide today." Xiaoman said nothing; his right hand stayed closed. She opened her notebook, wrote one line — **Thirty cash. Interest: none charged** — closed it, and said just two words: "Hide well."

That night, when everyone was asleep, Sun Ergou crept to Xiaoman's bunk and crouched a long while before he whispered: "Brother Shen. The first round… you lost on purpose, didn't you?" "No. My foot slipped." "The stones on the platform are dry." "My feet sweat." Sun Ergou said no more. He untied the blue pouch; the snapped string he'd already mended with thread, crooked. "Brother Shen, today I… fell seven times. Ma says falling down's no shame; not getting up is." He grinned, pulled at the cut on his chin, and hissed. "Seven times down on the stage, seven times up. Off the stage, when I sat on the steps… I really couldn't get up. You pulled me." Xiaoman said nothing. In the dark he heard Sun Ergou feel his way back to his bunk, and as he lay down he murmured: "…I'll remember." After a while his voice came again out of the dark: "Brother Shen, you can write, can't you?" "A few words." "Tomorrow… write a letter for me. My ma can't read; there's a teacher in the village who'll read it to her. Just write: Ma, I won a bout." A pause. "Don't write how."

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next

story.zh:
孙二狗走了以后，小满趴在铺上，就着窗外的月光，给家里写第一封信。他头一句写的是「娘，我当上仙人了」，擦了；第二句写「娘，我打赢了马小宝」，想了想，这话要是传到村里，马三怕是要上门，又擦了。

小满在铺上一笔一笔地写：**娘：我进仙门了。一年五两，观里说腊月就送到家。屋顶修一修。盆可以收起来了，十七个都收。给我爹买一副护膝，狗皮的。给吴婆婆，再送一条鹿腿，这回是买的。我在这里很好。有人欺负我，我记着账。有几笔，已经还上了。——小满**

握笔的是右手。月光底下，那个圈里一横贴着笔杆，凉凉的。他写完了，把那只手翻过来看了一会儿，又翻了回去。

小满把信折好，想了想，又打开来，在最底下添了一行：**娘，漏勺也能打水。**信压在枕头底下，明天一早交给周衡，跟沈家那一包五两银子一车送下山。弓就搁在枕头边上，他伸手摸了摸那十七道牛筋。他握着胸口的木牌，小声道：「你欠我的那张饼……还欠着吧？」木牌轻轻地，烫了一下。像是在说：**还欠着。**

隔了一会儿，木牌又烫了一下，这一回烫得发紧。银月的声音很低，一点也不懒：「镜子裂的那一下，镜子那头，有人。」小满一下子坐了起来：「哪头？」银月道：「很远。西边。本王只听见一句。」她顿了一顿，学那个声音，学得很平，平得没有一点起伏：「叫徐州那个，十月去邺城等着。」

小满在黑地里坐了很久。镜子裂的时候，镜子跟前站着的只有他一个；那道光往他胸口钻，钻着找的是木牌。徐州那个，就是他。他把右手翻过来，掌心那个圈里一横，凉凉的。邺城在哪里，他不知道。他摸出本子，就着月光，把这一句记在恩仇簿的最后一页，没有写是谁的账。
story.en:
When Sun Ergou had gone, Xiaoman lay on his bunk and by the moonlight at the window wrote his first letter home. The first line he wrote was "Ma, I've become an immortal" — rubbed out; the second, "Ma, I beat Ma Xiaobao" — he thought, if that got back to the village Ma San might come round, and rubbed it out too.

On his bunk Xiaoman wrote stroke by stroke: **Ma: I've entered the immortals' gate. Five taels a year; the temple says it'll reach home in the twelfth month. Fix the roof. The basins can be put away — all seventeen. Buy Pa a pair of kneepads, dog-skin. Send Granny Wu another leg of venison — bought, this time. I'm fine here. When people bully me, I keep accounts. A few are paid already. — Xiaoman**

He wrote with his right hand. In the moonlight the circle with its bar lay against the brush, cold. When he had finished he turned the hand over and looked at it a while, then turned it back.

Xiaoman folded the letter, thought, opened it again and added one line at the bottom: **Ma, a skimmer can carry water too.** He tucked it under his pillow; in the morning it would go to Zhou Heng and down the mountain on the same cart as the Shen family's five taels. The bow lay beside his pillow; he reached out and touched its seventeen wraps of sinew. Holding the token on his chest, he whispered: "That flatbread you owe me… still owed, right?" The token warmed, very lightly. As if to say: **Still owed.**

After a while the token burned again, tight this time. Yinyue's voice was low and not lazy at all: "The moment the mirror cracked — there was someone at the other end of it." Xiaoman sat straight up. "Which end?" "Far. West. I caught only one line." She paused, and copied the voice, very level, without a rise or fall in it: "Send the one from Xu. Tenth month, to Ye, to wait."

Xiaoman sat a long time in the dark. When the mirror cracked, he was the only one standing before it; the light had bored into his chest, and what it was looking for was the token. The one from Xu was him. He turned his right hand over: the ring with a bar across it in his palm, cool. Where Ye was, he didn't know. He took out his notebook and, by the moonlight, wrote the line on the last page of his ledger of debts, without writing whose debt it was.
